name: Widest banner between two posts
returns: a list of two whole numbers
brief:
Posts stand one metre apart along a trading-floor wall, and `posts[i]` is the height of post `i` in metres. A banner hangs between two posts `i < j`. Its width is `j - i` and its height is the shorter of the two posts, so its area is `min(posts[i], posts[j]) * (j - i)`.

Write `widest_banner(posts)`, which returns `[area, width]` for the banner with the largest area. If several banners share that area, return the widest of them. When no banner has an area above 0, including when there are fewer than two posts, return `[0, 0]`.

Example. For `posts = [2, 5, 1, 4]` the banner between the 5 and the 4 is 4 high and 2 wide, area 8. No pair does better, so the answer is `[8, 2]`.
constraints: $0 \le n \le 100{,}000$ posts, each a whole number between $0$ and $10^6$.
$O(n)$ time is the target. Trying every pair is too slow.
All the tests in a run share one 5-second limit in the browser.
hint: Start with the two end posts. The shorter of the pair caps every narrower banner that uses it, so move that pointer inwards. The walk meets the widest banners first, so only a strictly larger area should replace the best.

examples.note: The 5 and the 4 give 4 times 2. The two ends give only 2 times 3.
Two posts 1 metre apart, both 3 high, give area 3 and width 1.
The two 6s give area 6 at width 1, and the 6 and the 3 give 3 times 2, also 6. The wider banner is returned.

tests.call: widest_banner([1000000 - abs(50000 - i) for i in range(100001)])

how: Submit runs 14 hidden tests. Each answer must equal the expected value.
notes: Every narrower banner that keeps the shorter post is no taller and no wider, so that post can be dropped.
Moving the taller post instead can drop the best pair, as in `[3, 9, 4, 4, 2, 7, 5, 9, 1]`.
Each step drops one post, so the work is $O(n)$. The widest banners are met first, so a strict `>` keeps the widest of a tie.

planted.slip: Moving the taller post inwards can throw away the post that belongs to the best banner.
Counting posts, `j - i + 1`, instead of the gaps between them makes every banner one metre too wide.
Taking the taller post as the height lets the banner hang above the shorter post.
Replacing the best on `>=` lets a later, narrower banner of the same area win, so the returned width is too small.
